beginner.label: Beginner
beginner.description: Chord accompaniment: the bass note in the left hand and a triad in the right hand, one chord per bar.

original.label: Original
original.description: A fuller accompaniment: a bass arpeggio in the left hand and a held four-note chord in the right hand, notated on the grand staff.

analysis.title: Tonic
analysis.text: E major is the home chord, the one the other chords are measured against. The right hand holds its three notes with the root doubled on top.

analysis.title: Dominant
analysis.text: B major sits on the fifth degree of E major. Moving from the home chord to the fifth and back gives the intro and the verse their question-and-answer feel.

analysis.title: Relative minor
analysis.text: C# minor is the relative minor of E major. It shares two of its three notes, E and G#, with the home chord, so it sounds like a softer version of it.

analysis.title: Borrowed iv
analysis.text: A minor does not belong to E major, which has C# where A minor has C natural. The expected chord is A major (IV), so this Am is borrowed from the parallel key, E minor. This is called modal mixture. From C#m to Am the right hand moves only two voices by a half step: G# rises to A and C# falls to C, while E stays put.

analysis.title: C back to C#
analysis.text: From Am to A only one voice moves: C rises a half step to C#, and the sound turns major again. This is the first chord of the chorus, the part of the source with the lowest confidence.

analysis.title: Bass climbs
analysis.text: The bass note is A#, a half step above the A of the previous bar, so the bass climbs by a half step. F# major is the dominant of B (V of V), which is why the chord is labelled V6/V (first inversion). In this progression it moves on to C#m.

analysis.title: Supertonic
analysis.text: F#m is the chord on the second degree. In major keys a ii chord usually leads toward the dominant (B). Coming from Am, the C rises once more to C#.

beginner.summary: Cancer here is seven chords in a row: E, B, C#m, Am, A, F#/A# and F#m. Your left hand plays one low bass note and your right hand plays a three-note chord, one chord per bar, at a calm 72 BPM. It is a generic chord-based accompaniment, not a transcription of the recording.

handPositions.text: Finger numbers are the same on both hands: 1 is the thumb, 2 the index, 3 the middle, 4 the ring and 5 the little finger. Rest your thumb (1) on E4, your middle finger (3) on G#4 and your little finger (5) on B4, then press the three keys together. That is the E chord.
Put your left little finger (5) on the low E. The left hand only plays one note per bar, so keep it relaxed and let the little finger travel to the next bass note.
For the B chord the right hand steps down a little: thumb (1) on B3, middle finger (3) on D#4, little finger (5) on F#4. The left little finger plays B2.
C#m: thumb (1) on C#4, middle finger (3) on E4, little finger (5) on G#4. The left little finger plays C#3.
Am: thumb (1) on A3, middle finger (3) on C4, little finger (5) on E4. The left little finger plays A2. It sounds a little sadder than the chords before it.
A: the thumb stays on A3, and the middle finger (3) moves up to C#4. The little finger (5) stays on E4. The left little finger plays A2 again.
F#/A# means an F# chord with A# in the bass. Left little finger (5) on A#2; right thumb (1) on F#4, middle finger (3) on A#4, little finger (5) on C#5.
F#m: thumb (1) on F#3, middle finger (3) on A3, little finger (5) on C#4. The left little finger plays F#2.

beginner.posture: Sit toward the front half of the bench, centered on the keyboard, with your back straight but relaxed and your feet flat on the floor. Let your elbows hang a little in front of your body so that your forearms are level with the keys. Keep your wrists neither dropped nor lifted, and curve your fingers as if you were holding a small ball.
practicePlan: Sit as described and rest your hands on the keys without playing. Check that your shoulders are relaxed.
Practice hands separately. Press Mute right and play the left hand alone, one bass note per bar. Then press Mute left and play only the right-hand chords.
Turn on Slow and Metronome, pick Verse in Loop a section, and repeat it until the chord changes feel easy.
Play hands together at the slow tempo. When it feels comfortable, switch on Ramp so the tempo rises a little after each pass.
Finish with the Pre-Chorus and Chorus. Its chords are the least certain part of the source, so check them by ear.
beginner.arrangementNote: This is a generic chord-based accompaniment built from the chord progression: a bass note on the left and a triad on the right. It is not a transcription of the recording and it leaves out the vocal line.

original.summary: The Original level plays the same seven chords as Beginner with a fuller sound: the left hand plays a bass arpeggio and the right hand holds a four-note chord for the whole bar. It is a generic chord-based accompaniment, not a transcription of the recording. Turn on Analysis to read the harmony.

handPositions.text: Left hand: little finger (5) on E2, index finger (2) on B2, thumb (1) on E3, then the index finger back on B2. The same shape (root, fifth, octave, fifth) repeats on every chord.
Right hand: thumb (1) on E4, index finger (2) on G#4, middle finger (3) on B4 and little finger (5) on E5. Hold the four keys for the whole bar.

B chord: the thumb, index finger and little finger step down by one or two half steps while the middle finger stays on B4. Thumb (1) on D#4, index finger (2) on F#4, middle finger (3) on B4, little finger (5) on D#5.
C#m: every finger steps up from the B chord by one or two half steps. Thumb (1) on E4, index finger (2) on G#4, middle finger (3) on C#5, little finger (5) on E5.
Am: the thumb stays on E4, the index finger moves up to A4 and the middle finger moves down to C5. This is the borrowed chord: only two fingers change, each by a half step.
A: only the middle finger moves, from C5 up to C#5. Everything else stays where it was.
F#/A#: three fingers step up while the middle finger stays on C#5. Thumb (1) on F#4, index finger (2) on A#4, middle finger (3) on C#5, little finger (5) on F#5. The left hand starts on A#2.
F#m: thumb (1) on F#4, index finger (2) on A4, middle finger (3) on C#5, little finger (5) on F#5.

original.posture: Sit as in the Beginner lesson: centered, back straight but relaxed, forearms level with the keys. The right hand now holds an octave, so keep the hand open and the wrist level instead of pressing down.
practicePlan: Start with the left hand alone (press Mute right): four quarter notes per bar, root, fifth, octave, fifth. Switch on Metronome and keep it even.
Then press Mute left and practice moving the right-hand chord from bar to bar. Only one or two fingers change at each step, so look for the notes that stay.
Put the hands together with Slow on. Use Set A here and Set B here to loop bars 5 to 7 (C#m, Am, A) and listen to the borrowed Am.
Switch on Analysis to see the roman numerals and the notes about the harmony, then raise the tempo with Ramp.
original.arrangementNote: This is a generic chord-based accompaniment built from the chord progression: a bass arpeggio on the left and a held four-note chord on the right. It is not a transcription of the recording and it leaves out the vocal line. The chords come from one user-submitted source and the chorus is lower confidence.

sources.what: User-submitted chord progressions per section (Intro I V; Verse I V vi iv; Pre-Chorus and Chorus IV V6/V vi iv ii; a Bridge is listed and not used here), key E major, 4/4, 75 BPM. Chords only: no melody and no text were taken.
Key E major, common time and a tempo of 70 BPM (the article cites a Musicnotes sheet-music listing). No chords were taken from it.

confidence.note: One user-submitted source (Hooktheory) gives I V; it also tags seventh and add chords that this triad version leaves out.
One user-submitted source gives I V vi iv. Its page tags the verse with Borrowed Chords, so the fourth chord is the minor iv (Am), not the major IV; no second source confirms it.
One user-submitted source gives IV V6/V vi iv ii (F# over A#, then Am, then F#m). No second source agrees and the inversion and the minor iv are the least certain parts.
The sources list progressions, not bar counts. One chord per bar and the section lengths are an editorial layout for practice.
Sources disagree slightly: 70 BPM (Wikipedia) and 75 BPM (Hooktheory). The default of 72 sits between them; the practice range is 70 to 75.

Editorial on both levels: Beginner uses root-position triads with fingers 1, 3 and 5 in the right hand and finger 5 on the bass note; Original uses 5, 2, 1, 2 in the left hand and 1, 2, 3, 5 in the right hand.
Editorial: the Original voicings and the root, fifth, octave, fifth bass pattern are an arrangement choice built only from the notes of each chord. They are not taken from any source.

The analysis describes the chords as listed in the chord track, so it is only as certain as they are (the chorus is lower confidence). The theory terms used (relative minor, modal mixture, secondary dominant) are standard.
